newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK retail sales to rise steadily in Nov.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK retail sales to rise steadily in Nov.

text.p: Anecdotal evidence from Britain's crowded high streets suggests retail sales chalked up another month of steady growth in November, analysts said on Monday.
A Reuter poll of economists found a consensus expected a 0.5 percent rise in sales on the month, leaving them 3.4 percent higher than a year earlier.
The figures will be released at 0930 GMT on Wednesday.
The annual performance may look a little subdued compared with October's 4.1 percent year-on-year rise but that is due to a hefty leap in sales expenditure last November, analysts said.

"The CBI distributive trades and British Retail Consortium Surveys both pointed to a slowdown in retail sales in November," said David Philpotts, economist at Schroders. "But this should hardly be surprising given that both are expressed relative to 12 months previously."

The Confederation of British Industry's last distributive trades survey showed the balance of firms reporting higher sales than in November 1995 fell to 48 percent, from 55 in October. In addition, the BRC's sales monitor showed retail sales grew 4.9 percent year-on-year in value terms in November. The month before, sales were up 5.9 percent.

But both those surveys would have suffered from the bumper November retailers enjoyed last year. The underlying picture remains firm to say the least. "The CBI's evidence is consistent with a buoyant rise in sales this month," said Philip Uglow, economist at Union Plc. "Data from the BRC paints a different picture though, suggesting that volumes may actually have fallen back in November."
He forecast a small 0.2 percent rise in November sales.
Philpotts said one factor that could have subdued sales last month was the sharp increase in clothing and footwear and household goods prices.
Retail price data released last week showed clothing and footwear prices leapt 1.1 percent in November while household goods prices jumped 1.0 percent.
"That could have triggered some resistance from consumers who are used to price discounts," Philpotts said.
John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International, said consumers may have held fire on high street spending ahead of Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's November 26 budget.
But whether November proves to have been a subdued one for retailers or not, he forecast a Christmas sales bonanza.

"Now consumers have got tax cuts, a rising housing market and falling unemployment, and interest rates are not going up as quickly as thought. All the evidence adds up to a bumper Christmas," Shepperd said.
Independent consultants Verdict predict a 7.7 percent increase this December over last year. That translates into about an extra 20 billion pounds ($32.86 billion) pouring into shop tills.
